title: x86 TSO versus ARM memory ordering
hook: Why does code that works on x86 TSO break on ARM's weaker memory model?

scenes.caption: x86-TSO only lets a later load pass an earlier store, via the store buffer.
scenes.narration: x86 provides total store order. Loads aren't reordered with loads, stores aren't reordered with stores, and the only visible reordering is a load passing an older store to another address.

scenes.caption: ARM64 allows loads and stores to be reordered with each other unless ordered by dependency or barrier.
scenes.narration: ARM is weakly ordered. Independent loads and stores may become visible in any order, so the same lock-free code can behave differently, unless you add barriers or acquire and release.

items: Order only via deps or barriers

scenes.caption: Message passing: data then flag works on x86 but can read stale data on ARM.
scenes.narration: Consider a writer that stores data then sets a flag. On x86 the reader that sees the flag always sees the data. On ARM the stores can become visible out of order.

elements.text: Plain C: a data race on both.

scenes.caption: Fix: release-store the flag and acquire-load it with C11 atomics.
scenes.narration: The portable fix is release on the flag store and acquire on the flag load. The compiler emits nothing special on x86, but on ARM64 it emits stlr and ldar.

scenes.caption: x86 compiles these to plain mov; ARM64 uses stlr and ldar, and full fences need dmb ish.
scenes.narration: The same source maps to different instructions. x86 uses ordinary mov for release and acquire, while ARM64 uses stlr and ldar. A sequentially consistent fence is mfence on x86, dmb ish on ARM.

elements.text: Full fence: mfence vs dmb ish

takeaway: x86 hides ordering bugs behind a strong model; on ARM you must state your intent with acquire, release or barriers.
